extracted.intended_audience: physicians and legal professionals (doctors, surgeons, lawyers)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and professional standards governing physicians' liability: the implied contractual duties, required standard of skill and care, negligence and criminal exposure, patient duties and defenses, and rules on departures from established practice (with examples and case-law distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician's implied contractual duties
rubrics_metrics.description: In undertaking the care of a patient the physician enters into legal relations and a contract (though not necessarily written) that he possesses a reasonable degree of learning, skill, and experience ordinarily possessed by the professors of the same art or science, and that he will employ reasonable and ordinary care and diligence in the exertion of his skill and application of his knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational obligation: breach permits civil action for malpractice. The page states the physician "engages that he possesses that reasonable degree of learning, skill, and experience..." and "contracts also to employ reasonable and ordinary care and diligence." Examples and citations given (e.g., T. Foster, New Hampshire, 460).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of care — ordinary skill and care (not extraordinary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician is held to the ordinary degree of learning, skill, and experience ordinarily possessed by others in the profession; extraordinary skill or extraordinary care is not contracted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the physician has employed ordinary skill and care in management, he is not responsible if success does not follow; but if he lacks ordinary skill or fails to employ it, he is liable. The text: "If the physician has employed ordinary skill and care... he is not responsible if success does not crown his efforts. But... if he does not bring... the ordinary amount of skill... it is immaterial how high his standing may be. He is liable for the want of it."

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liability requires only negligence (not gross culpability)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary, to sustain an action for malpractice, that there should be proof of gross culpability; ordinary negligence suffices to impose civil liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes physicians are on the same footing as other professionals performing services requiring skill and care: failures to exercise proper care or negligence can create liability even absent gross wrongdoing. "He is on the same footing, and subject to the same degree of liability, as any other person..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for gross negligence or want of care (manslaughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patient's death is presumptively caused by treatment and the practitioner is guilty of gross rashness, gross ignorance, gross negligence, or criminal inattention, criminal proceedings (e.g., manslaughter) may be instituted; malicious intent may be inferred from gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that while malicious intent may be absent, the law may infer it from gross carelessness. Quotation: in England, one who professes to deal with life or health and causes death through a 'gross want' of skill or attention 'will be guilty of manslaughter.' Examples: gross errors leading to criminal charges are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for conscientious errors of judgment in cases of reasonable doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician is not contracted for freedom from all errors of judgment; one possessing ordinary skill is presumed to have ordinary good judgment, and if fairly and conscientiously exercised in a case of reasonable doubt and uncertainty, errors are upon the patient (i.e., not actionable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits liability where judgment calls are made reasonably and in good faith. The author contrasts errors of judgment with negligence or lack of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability continues after case termination (retirement, failure to bill, gratuitous service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retiring from the case does not shield the physician from liability for prior negligence; failure to send a bill might be interpreted as admission of neglect; rendering services gratuitously is not necessarily a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: "Once having incurred the liability, it sticks... Retiring from the case is of no avail... Nor will neglect to send in a bill... It has been held also that it is no defense that the services were rendered gratuitously." These are practical anti-defenses to malpractice claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient's duty to cooperate and contributory negligence defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The patient has a duty to cooperate with the physician and conform to necessary prescriptions; if the patient's neglect to obey reasonable instructions contributes to the injury, he cannot recover (contributory negligence is a good defense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a patient failing to keep an arm in the required position after reduction led to no recovery where surgeon had given proper directions; conversely, if the physician lulled the patient into a false sense of security and that caused refusal/cooperation failure, the physician may be liable. The text compares the patient to a pedestrian on railroad tracks to illustrate contributory negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to give adequate instructions/warnings (post-treatment directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A physician who omits necessary warnings or instructions (e.g., that an arm must remain in a particular position) may be culpably negligent even if the physical procedure itself was properly performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the specific surgical example where omission to warn the patient that the arm must remain in position was held culpable negligence. This criterion emphasizes communication/instructions as part of the standard of care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability when physician's assurances or guarantees cause patient reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the physician guarantees a successful issue, he will be held responsible for failure to effect a cure, even though ordinarily he would not be liable if he had employed reasonable care and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees or express promises of success raise strict responsibility beyond ordinary standard of care. The text asks rhetorically about weight of assurances from a negligent physician and states guarantees create liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on liability for external or patient-specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability is limited where adverse outcome is due to factors the physician is expected to guard against but which may not be controllable: latent predispositions, lack of recuperative power, mental state, poor air/food/nursing, or patient non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists these as considerations that may absolve or mitigate physician liability: "His diligence and care will be exercised in watching for and guarding against... latent predisposition... want of vital or recuperative power... the effect of melancholy... want of pure air and good food... the neglect of the patient to follow the physician's advice." These are defenses or mitigating factors in causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician liable if patient refuses further remedial treatment because of physician's conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patient refuses necessary precautions or further remedial attempts because he was lulled into a sense of security by the doctor, the doctor will be liable; refusal to undergo remedial attempts after malpractice does not necessarily preclude recovery if the refusal was without reasonable assurance of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deals with causation and mitigation: if the doctor's assurances lead patient to decline further care, the doctor may remain liable. Conversely, if refusal was unreasonable the patient may be barred. The page distinguishes reasonable vs unreasonable refusals and mentions that refusal without reasonable assurance of success does not preclude recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on deviation from established practice / experimental treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a strict (English) rule, any deviation from established rules of practice renders the practitioner liable; American authorities modify this: adopting a different system of treatment is not negligence if others have applied it successfully — but adopting a novel/experimental treatment is at the physician's peril unless it has been previously tested and found successful in substantially similar cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques the English rule as too harsh and details the American modification: one cannot be an experimentalist except at his peril; but if others have practically tested and found a different system to succeed 'as well as or better than' the prescribed one, it may be followed safely, provided cases are substantially same and success sufficient to justify adoption.
